2U CubeSat structure redesign

LEARNSat mechanical team member, UGA Small Satellite Research Lab. Sept. 2026 to present. Inventor, Siemens NX, FEA.

A bolted frame built from two part types, stiffened by making the side panels carry load.

260 Hz
predicted first mode, up from 190 Hz
2
unique machined part types
0.34 kg
structure mass
±0.1 mm
rail flatness

Problem

The team needed a new 2U primary structure inside the standard 100 × 100 × 227 mm envelope. A plain bolted frame is cheap to machine but soft, and its joints can slip under launch vibration.

What we did

  • Built the frame from two unique part types: four identical 6061-T6 rails and two identical end plates.
  • Made the side panels structural, bolted at a close pitch so they carry shear.
  • Located the rail-to-plate joints with dowel pins in reamed holes.
  • Compared the options in FEA before committing.

Result

The predicted first mode rose from 190 to 260 Hz. Two part types about halved machining cost compared with a one-piece cage, and peak launch stress stays under a quarter of yield.

Trade-off

The frame is slightly heavier than a one-piece cage and takes more assembly steps. In return, a damaged part can be swapped without remaking the frame.

Autonomous vehicle hardware

Mechanical lead, Heterogeneous Robotics (HeRo) Lab, UGA, Athens, GA. June 2026 to present. Fusion 360, 3D printing on a Creality K1C.

I design and 3D print the robots' parts, their charging dock, and the overhead traffic light at the intersection they drive through.

Problem

The lab runs four small autonomous Moorebot robots through a tabletop smart city. The robots were heavier than they needed to be, their pressure-contact charging was unreliable, and the intersection needed an overhead traffic light their cameras could see.

What I did

  • Charging dock. Led a team of 3 to make all 4 robots autodock with a 3D printed magnetic charging dock, replacing the old pressure contacts. The dock's upright wall holds the mating connectors at the height of the robot's.
  • Robot housing. Designed the bolt-on Moorebot housing: a top plate and a rear bracket that holds two magnetic pogo-pin connectors. When the robot backs in, magnets pull the connectors onto the dock's positive and negative contacts.
  • Wiring. Soldered the connectors and rerouted the wiring over the top plate with the electrical team so the robots can back in and charge.
  • Lighter vehicles. Redesigned the chassis and the wheels in Fusion 360 over 8 iterations. Each drive wheel is a PLA hub with three triangular cutouts, wrapped in a grooved TPU tire for grip.
  • Traffic light. Designed a 41-piece overhead traffic light in Fusion 360, rebuilt over 4 revisions for camera line of sight. A Raspberry Pi in a case at the foot of one leg drives it, with the wiring run up through the hollow tubes to a center housing that has lights on all four sides. The robots' cameras read those lights, so they stop and go like traffic in a miniature automated city.

Result

Vehicle mass dropped 15%, and all 4 robots now dock and charge on their own.

Aircraft

Hoerner wing tip CFD study

Aerodynamics team member, AIAA Design Build Fly, UGA. November 2026. Ansys Fluent 2026 R1 (Student), SpaceClaim, Fluent Meshing, Fusion 360.

A full CFD run, from CAD to results, of an E214 wing with a Hoerner tip at 15 m/s and 4° angle of attack, to see how the tip shapes the vortex and the drag.

0.547
lift coefficient
0.0646
drag coefficient
8.5
lift-to-drag ratio
589,664
cells in the mesh

Problem

A Hoerner tip is a sharp, swept-up wingtip meant to push the tip vortex outboard and cut induced drag, the drag the vortex causes. I wanted to see that flow, and to run the whole CFD workflow myself: clean the geometry, build the air domain, mesh it, solve it, and turn the results into pictures that explain the tip.

What I did

  • Full workflow. Built a complete CFD workflow that converged in 132 iterations with every residual below 1 × 10⁻⁵, by taking a Fusion 360 wing through SpaceClaim, Fluent Meshing, and the Fluent solver in Workbench.
  • Lift and drag. Predicted a lift coefficient of 0.547 and a drag coefficient of 0.0646 (L/D about 8.5) at a Reynolds number near 100,000, by solving half the wing on a symmetry plane with the k-ω SST model. I tilted the incoming air instead of the wing, so one mesh works for any angle.
  • Boundary layer. Resolved the air layer at the wall directly, with y+ no higher than 2.36 and below 1 over most of the wing, by hand-calculating a 0.02 mm first-cell height from a flat-plate skin-friction estimate and growing 15 thin layers off the surface.
  • Mesh. Built a 589,664-cell poly-hexcore mesh with a minimum orthogonal quality of 0.16 and maximum surface skewness of 0.53, by re-exporting the CAD with the trailing edge thickened from 0.01 mm to 0.4 mm and the sliver along the tip edge made tall enough for the layers to fit.
  • Checks. Confirmed the setup was consistent, shown by a pressure coefficient of exactly 1.00 at the stagnation point, and kept the force totals complete by finding a 0.61 mm² nose face missing from the wing selection and adding it to the lift and drag reports.
  • Where the drag comes from. Estimated that about 85% of the drag is induced, the part a Hoerner tip is meant to reduce, by comparing the CFD drag with a hand calculation of induced drag for the wing's aspect ratio of about 2.1.

What the results show

Most of the lift comes from a suction band (pressure coefficient down to about −1.4) along the top leading edge. A second suction strip runs along the sharp tip edge, where air speeds up as it wraps around. That air leaks from the high-pressure underside onto the top and rolls into a vortex that drifts slightly up and outboard behind the wing.

Limits and next steps

This is one mesh at one condition, not yet checked against wind-tunnel data. The SST model treats the flow as turbulent from the nose, so at this Reynolds number friction drag is probably overestimated. The model is also a short wing (aspect ratio about 2), so lift sits below 2D airfoil data. Next: measure the true planform area in Fusion, rerun with Transition SST, run a mesh-independence check and an angle-of-attack sweep, and simulate a plain square tip for a direct comparison.

Aircraft

Towed sensor stability

Aerodynamics team member, AIAA Design Build Fly, UGA. April 2026 to present. Barrowman method, Python, Fusion 360.

A 23 lb sensor that hangs from the aircraft on a cable and has to fly straight, like a dart.

+0.79
calibers of static margin, up from +0.06
460
fin, flare, and nose combinations swept
23 lb
sensor, towed on a cable

Problem

The sensor is 3 in wide, 12 in long, and 23 lb. It never needs lift. It only has to point into the wind and not tumble on the cable.

What I did

  • Used the Barrowman method to find the center of pressure and the static margin.
  • Swept 460 fin, flare, and nose combinations, then set fin span and flare diameter at the box limit.
  • Moved the electronics aft of the lead ballast, which brought the center of gravity forward.
  • Hung the sensor from a pylon over its center of gravity so gravity keeps it level in pitch.
  • Chose a steel tube over PVC, copper, and aluminum.

Result

Static margin rose from +0.06 to +0.79 calibers. A tow test is the next check.

Guided rocket flight computer

Personal project. May 2026 to present. Python. Code on GitHub

Software that decides when a model rocket should fire its parachute, using noisy sensors.

0.21 ft
mean apogee error
20
simulated flights
5

Problem

A rocket has to fire its parachute at the top of its flight. Fire too early or too late and the rocket is damaged, and the sensors it relies on are noisy.

What I did

  • Wrote a Python flight simulation with simulated barometer and motion sensor data.
  • Built a Kalman filter that combines both sensors to estimate altitude and speed.
  • Wrote a state machine that fires the parachute 0.2 s early to cover the igniter delay.
  • Tested it across 20 randomized flights and with sensor dropouts.

Result

Mean apogee error is 0.21 ft. I root-caused 5 defects along the way. The next step is porting the code to an ESP32.

Problem

Design a 4U CubeSat structure that meets the CubeSat Design Specification and is cheap to machine and easy to assemble.

What I did

  • Designed a five-part Al 6061-T6 frame in Inventor, merging the rails and panels into one tube.
  • Checked the frame at an 8.5 g launch load with hand calculations and FEA.
  • Chose 6061-T6 over 7075 for cheaper machining.
  • Specified press fits, Helicoil inserts, and anodizing.

Result

The frame shows a 3.0 factor of safety at the launch load. That margin is why 7075's extra strength wasn't worth its cost.

Spacecraft

CanSat egg protector

CanSat Competition 2026: Paraglider Instrument Delivery. In progress. One printed PETG part, plus foam.

The payload has to release a hen's egg 2 m above the ground without breaking it. The egg stands in for a delicate instrument. I designed the part that holds and protects it.

1.5 mm
clearance around the egg
4
equator spokes holding the mesh
14 mm
free gap at each pole
30 G
shock it has to survive

Problem

In the 2026 mission, a paraglider payload steers to a target, then releases a protected hen's egg at 2 m ± 0.5 m above the ground. The egg must not break (requirement C12). The egg device also has to survive 15 G vibration and 30 G shock (S8, S9), use hard-mounted components (S17), and keep its state under all forces (M3). The whole CanSat must weigh 1000 g ± 10 g (S1).

What I designed

It has three jobs: hold the egg securely, absorb the impact, and survive the flight loads.

  • Inner mesh. PETG ribs and rings hug the egg with about 1.5 mm of clearance, so it can't rattle or bounce out. That's the failure people report most often in egg drops. The open mesh keeps mass low and lets you see the egg.
  • Four equator spokes. They hold the mesh in the middle of the cage. They were meant to let it move slightly and cushion the hit (S9), while keeping everything hard mounted (S17).
  • Square grid cage. Posts, a mid frame, and end plates form the rigid outer structure. It carries the flight and landing loads, protects the mesh, and gives a clear interface to the rest of the CanSat. The grid windows save mass and let the whole cage print as one PETG piece.
  • Free gap at each pole. 14 mm of room for the mesh and egg to slow down after the cage hits the ground.

What it does and doesn't do yet

It holds the egg centered, keeps it contained, carries the structural loads, and is easy to print, inspect, and explain. As built, it can't reliably protect the egg in the 2 m drop. The PETG spokes are stiff, so the mesh barely moves and the egg gets almost no stopping distance.

Next

I added foam. Now the foam absorbs the impact, and the PETG is the structure that holds the foam in place. My numbers so far are rough estimates, not test results. Drop testing is next.

Problem

Under the federal Safe Streets and Roads for All program, a city or county writes a safety action plan before it can get money to fix its roads. The plan has to show where people are being killed and seriously hurt, and what to do about it.

What I did

  • Mapped high-injury road networks and recommended safety fixes for 5 federally funded projects.
  • Made the maps and charts in these plans, including crash density maps, High Injury Network maps, and crash summary graphics.
  • Built an ArcPy GIS tool that cut manual review from 5 hours to 3 per project at 98% spatial accuracy.
  • Presented findings to city and state officials and the public at stakeholder and public meetings.

Dublin, Georgia

The plan covered 3,538 crashes from 2020 to 2024, including 89 that killed or seriously injured someone. Its High Injury Network found that 59% of crashes happened on 8% of the city's roads. The city adopted the plan in May 2026. Read the executive summary (PDF)

Clay County, Florida

At the October 2025 public meeting at the Fleming Island Library, crash maps were set up around the room so residents could point out the roads they see as problems. See the Clay County plan document, or read the News4JAX coverage.

Pecos City, Texas

Bilingual crash mapping and safety analysis boards for the town's public meetings.
